title: Geometry-controlled zeros of resonant Kelvin-wave conversion in four spatial dimensions
authors: Wei-can Yang, Xiang-dong Xu, Cheng Li
abstract: Kelvin waves carry energy along vortices, but their resonant interactions contain information that is absent from the linear spectrum. We identify a geometry that exposes this information on a vortex surface in four spatial dimensions. Perpendicular incoming waves cancel the complete local-area four-wave coupling, leaving the finite nonlocal interaction mediated by the surrounding fluid. This interaction restores conversion at generic wave-number ratios, yet changes sign and vanishes at a selected ratio while momentum and frequency remain exactly matched. Matching to Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) theory, including the microscopic core response, establishes a zero of the full coupling at every sufficiently small nonzero wave number, with ratio tending to $λ_*\simeq1.469$. Finite-grid GP coefficients exhibit a sign reversal for the same resonant quartets. Separate coherent-mixing calculations and weak-probe spectra connect the coupling sign to the generated-wave phase and the ordering of reflection-even and reflection-odd modes. The resulting suppression removes a leading channel for changing propagation directions without changing the paired wavelengths. These results isolate a nonlinear effect of the surrounding flow that local tension misses, providing a microscopic benchmark for vortex-wave theories and a starting point for studying angular redistribution beyond the Kelvin spectrum.
summary: This paper investigates resonant energy conversion in Kelvin waves propagating along vortices in superfluids in four dimensions. By comparing the full Gross-Pitaevskii theory with non-local fluid dynamics, the authors pinpoint a specific geometry that forces the four-wave coupling coefficient to zero at a critical wave-number ratio ($\lambda^* \simeq 1.469$). This zero highlights a crucial nonlinear effect mediated by the surrounding fluid flow.
main_problem: To identify a geometry that exposes information about resonant Kelvin-wave interactions, which is absent from the linear spectrum, in four spatial dimensions.
main_result: The analysis establishes a zero in the leading four-wave coupling coefficient at a critical wave-number ratio $\lambda^* \simeq 1.469$, isolating a nonlinear effect of the surrounding fluid flow.
method: The authors compare the full Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) action with the non-local interaction derived from the surrounding fluid flow, using limit analysis ($q 	o 0$) to find matching conditions.
model_or_system: The system involves Kelvin waves propagating along vortices in superfluids, modeled using the GP equation and analyzed in four spatial dimensions. The core physics revolves around resonant four-wave coupling mediated by the surrounding fluid.
key_observables: The coupling coefficient $g_{GP}(q, \lambda)$ and the finite nonlocal interaction coefficient $f(\lambda)$; the zero location $\lambda^* \simeq 1.469$.
important_parameters: Wave-number ratio $\lambda$, the small wave number $q$, and the critical ratio $\lambda^*$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to match the complete Kelvin modes and intermediate responses between the GP and fluid actions, and that the zero found is for the leading four-wave coupling.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the quartet resonance structure and the finite coefficient $f(\lambda)$ with its first zero at $\lambda^* \simeq 1.469$. Figure 2 compares GP and fluid theories showing sign-change intervals, and Figure 3 illustrates coherent mixing in the GP model.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the local and non-local interactions, selecting a geometry that cancels local coupling, calculating the resulting nonlocal interaction via fluid theory, and finally matching this result to the full GP theory to locate the resonant zero.
why_interesting: This work provides a microscopic benchmark for vortex-wave theories, detailing how non-local fluid effects can suppress specific nonlinear coupling channels that are missed by simpler local tension models.
